title: SAR narrative: the five essential elements (who, what, when, where, why) plus how
text:
Source: FinCEN, "Guidance on Preparing A Complete & Sufficient Suspicious Activity Report Narrative," November 2003. https://www.fincen.gov/system/files/shared/sar_guidance_narrative.pdf (this same guidance is also linked in README1.md as "Preparing a Complete and Sufficient SAR Narrative")

"In general, a SAR narrative should identify the five essential elements of information – who? what? when? where? and why? – of the suspicious activity being reported. The method of operation (or how?) is also important and should be included in the narrative."

- **Who**: describe the suspect(s) beyond the form's dedicated fields — occupation, position/title, nature of their business, known relationships between multiple suspects, all known addresses (including PO boxes/apartment numbers), and any identification numbers (passport, alien registration, driver's license).
- **What**: the instruments or mechanisms used (wire transfers, letters of credit, correspondent accounts, structuring, shell companies, bonds/notes, stocks, insurance policies, travelers checks, bank drafts, money orders, credit/debit cards, stored value cards, digital currency services), the method of initiating the transaction (Internet, phone, mail, night deposit, remote dial-up, couriers), and always the source and application (origination and beneficiary use) of the funds.
- **When**: the date the activity was first noticed and its duration; individual dates and amounts of transactions should be included rather than just an aggregated total. Do not insert tables, spreadsheets, or other objects into the narrative — they may not convert properly when keyed into the SAR System.
- **Where**: whether multiple offices of the institution were involved (with addresses), and whether the activity involves a foreign jurisdiction (name the jurisdiction, institution, address, and account numbers).
- **Why**: describe the filer's own industry/business first, then explain as fully as possible why the activity is unusual for this customer, considering the products/services offered and the normally expected activity of similar customers.
- **How**: describe the "modus operandi" — how the suspect transaction or pattern was committed, in a concise, accurate, logical manner, giving as complete a picture as possible (e.g. if structuring is matched with outgoing wire transfers, describe both, including dates, destinations, amounts, accounts, frequency, and beneficiaries).

title: SAR narrative structure: introduction, body, conclusion
text:
Source: FinCEN, "Guidance on Preparing A Complete & Sufficient Suspicious Activity Report Narrative," November 2003.

"We suggest that you divide the narrative into three sections: an introduction, a body, and a conclusion."

- **Introduction** can provide: the purpose of the SAR and a general description of the known or alleged violation; the date of any previously filed SAR(s) on the suspect and why; whether the SAR is associated with OFAC's sanctioned countries, Specially Designated Nationals, or other government lists; any internal investigative reference number; and a summary of the "red flags" and suspicious patterns that initiated the SAR.
- **Body** can provide: all relevant facts about the parties who facilitated the activity (including unusual observations like suspected shell entities or activity inconsistent with expected business flows); a specific description of the involved accounts and transactions in chronological order by date and amount; transactor and beneficiary information (names, addresses, account numbers, involved institutions); any observed relationships among the transactors; specific cash transaction details (branch, type, how conducted); and any factual observations or incriminating statements made by the suspect.
- **Conclusion** can summarize the report and include: any follow-up action taken by the institution (e.g. account closure, ongoing monitoring); additional contacts at the institution; a description of further information that may be made available to law enforcement; and names of any law enforcement personnel already involved.

"Please do not include any supporting documentation with your filed report nor use the terms 'see attached' in the Narrative Section." Only explicit narrative-format text is entered into the SAR System database — tables, spreadsheets, and attachments are not. Keep supporting documentation in the institution's own records instead (see the retention chunk below).

title: Account takeover: definition and attack methods
text:
Source: FinCEN Advisory FIN-2011-A016, "Account Takeover Activity." https://www.fincen.gov/resources/advisories/fincen-advisory-fin-2011-a016

Account takeover occurs when cybercriminals gain unauthorized access to customer accounts, where "the customer, rather than the financial institution maintaining the account, is the primary target," with the goal of removing or stealing customer funds. Criminals employ techniques such as malware, SQL injection attacks, spyware, Trojans, and worms to gain seemingly legitimate account access.

title: Account takeover: red flags and SAR filing guidance
text:
Source: FinCEN Advisory FIN-2011-A016, "Account Takeover Activity."

Financial institutions should monitor for irregularities including: unusual ATM activity, clustered ACH transactions across different geographic areas, sudden wire transfers, and changes to customer and account profiles.

When filing a SAR connected to this advisory: use "account takeover fraud" terminology in the narrative; check the "computer intrusion" box if applicable, plus "other"; for wire transfers, check both "wire transfer fraud" and "other"; for ACH transfers, note "account takeover fraud - ACH"; consider the "identity theft" checkbox if unauthorized PINs or account numbers were accessed.

title: Money mule schemes: unwitting, witting, and complicit mules
text:
Source: FinCEN Advisory FIN-2020-A003, "Advisory on Imposter Scams and Money Mule Schemes Related to Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19)," July 7, 2020. https://www.fincen.gov/system/files/advisory/2020-07-07/Advisory_%20Imposter_and_Money_Mule_COVID_19_508_FINAL.pdf

A money mule is "a person who transfers illegally acquired money on behalf of or at the direction of another." Money mule schemes span a spectrum:

- **Unwitting/unknowing**: "unaware that he or she is part of a larger criminal scheme," motivated by trust in an actual romance, job position, or proposition.
- **Witting**: "chooses to ignore obvious red flags or acts willfully blind to his/her money movement activity," motivated by financial gain or unwillingness to acknowledge their role.
- **Complicit**: "aware of his/her role as a money mule and is complicit in the larger criminal scheme," motivated by financial gain or loyalty to a criminal group.

Recruiters have used good-Samaritan, romance, and work-from-home schemes, and have exploited unemployment insurance programs.

title: Money mule schemes: financial red flag indicators
text:
Source: FinCEN Advisory FIN-2020-A003.

- A personal account starts receiving transactions inconsistent with the customer's transactional history (overseas transactions, large convertible-virtual-currency purchases, large fiat amounts, or a previously low balance), and the customer declines KYC requests or cites a "work-from-home" opportunity as the source.
- A new business account receives funds that are transferred out shortly after opening, with the transferor keeping a portion per a third party's instruction.
- Accounts opened at multiple banks in one person's name to receive money from various sources, then move it onward at a purported employer's direction.
- Multiple state unemployment insurance payments received in the same disbursement timeframe from one or multiple states, or from a state where the customer doesn't reside/work.
- Deposited funds quickly diverted via wire to foreign accounts in countries with poor anti-money-laundering controls.
- A purported employer/recruiter using a free, non-company email address rather than an organization-specific one.
- The customer is asked to receive funds into their personal account so the "employer" can process or transfer them onward via wire, ACH, mail, or a money services business.
- Requests for financial assistance from a previously unknown individual claiming to be a U.S. service member stationed abroad, a U.S. citizen working/traveling abroad, or a U.S. citizen quarantined abroad.

title: Imposter scams: red flag indicators
text:
Source: FinCEN Advisory FIN-2020-A003.

An imposter scam involves an actor "(1) contacting a target under the false pretense of representing an official organization, and (2) coercing or convincing the target to provide funds or valuable information, engage in behavior that causes the target's computer to be infected with malware, or spread disinformation." Red flags include: a customer reporting contact from someone claiming to represent a government agency and requesting personal/bank information to "verify, process, or expedite" benefits; receipt of a document resembling a government check/prepaid card with instructions to call a number to "verify" personal information; unsolicited communications asking the recipient to open embedded links/files or provide account credentials; sender email addresses that don't match the claimed organization's domain, or that are misspelled; and charitable solicitations from an org with no verifiable history, financial reports, or tax-exempt documentation.

title: SAR filing threshold and structuring
text:
Source: FinCEN, Federal Reserve, FDIC, NCUA, OCC — "Frequently Asked Questions Regarding Suspicious Activity Reporting Requirements," October 9, 2025. https://www.fincen.gov/system/files/2025-10/SAR-FAQs-October-2025.pdf

A transaction at or near the $10,000 CTR threshold does not by itself require a SAR: "Financial institutions are only required to file a SAR if the institution knows, suspects, or has reason to suspect that the transaction or series of transactions are designed to evade CTR reporting requirements." A SAR is required for a transaction involving or aggregating at least $5,000 when the institution knows, suspects, or has reason to suspect it is designed to evade a BSA reporting requirement — including structuring, defined as conducting one or more currency transactions, in any amount, at one or more institutions, on one or more days, "in any manner," for the purpose of evading CTR reporting. This explicitly includes breaking a sum above $10,000 into smaller sums at or below $10,000.

title: Continuing suspicious activity: 90-day filing guidance
text:
Source: FinCEN et al., "Frequently Asked Questions Regarding Suspicious Activity Reporting Requirements," October 9, 2025.

A financial institution is not required to conduct a separate review of a customer/account after filing a SAR to check whether the activity continued — risk-based internal monitoring is sufficient. Institutions that do elect to follow FinCEN's continuing-activity guidance use this timeline (subject identified case): Day 0 — detection of facts that may support a SAR; Day 30 — filing of the initial SAR; Day 120 — end of the 90-day period; Day 150 — filing of a SAR for continued activity. (If no subject can be identified and the institution uses the extra 30 days allowed for that, every date shifts by 30 days.) There is no requirement to document a decision *not* to file a SAR, though FinCEN has encouraged doing so with a short, concise statement.

title: SAR supporting documentation: retention and disclosure requirements
text:
Source: FinCEN Guidance FIN-2007-G003, "Suspicious Activity Report Supporting Documentation," June 13, 2007. https://www.fincen.gov/system/files/shared/fin-2007-g003.pdf

A financial institution must maintain a copy of the SAR and the original (or business-record equivalent) of any supporting documentation for five years from the date of filing, and must provide it on request to FinCEN or an appropriate law enforcement or supervisory agency. "Supporting documentation" is "all documents or records that assisted a financial institution in making the determination that certain activity required a SAR filing" — e.g. transaction records, new account information, tape recordings, e-mail messages, and correspondence; a record can qualify even if not named in the narrative. It must not be attached to the SAR filing itself. Disclosure of supporting documentation to FinCEN or an appropriate agency does not require legal process (unlike most financial-record requests under the Right to Financial Privacy Act) and is protected by BSA safe-harbor provisions from civil liability.
